On January [XXX], 2023, RRAI received a support request through their Customer Support Portal from Beep, Inc., the owner of the vehicle, regarding their Olli 2.0 vehicle bumping into the curb in Peachtree Corners, GA. At 11:01 am, while running the normal route, the Olli contacted the adjacent curb on the front right side, causing tie rod and cosmetic damage. No one was injured and the only damage was to the vehicle itself. The customer contacted RRAI through the client support portal shortly after the incident. No injuries occurred, there were no passengers besides the safety operator, no other vehicles were involved, and no emergency systems were engaged.
Olli 2.0 (S/N 2-18) is an 8-passenger shuttle that is no longer manufactured. The vehicle manufacturer, Local Motors, dissolved in 2022. Local Motors contracted RRAI to install autonomy kits for several Olli shuttles during the period of 2018 - 2020. RRAI provided some support for initial site deployment and ensured customer safety operators were trained on the autonomy system. Since the Local Motors dissolution in 2022, almost all Olli vehicles have been decommissioned.
To date, we have concluded the following:
1. There were no updates or alterations made by RRAI in the months prior to Jan [XXX]. In previous operations, including the immediately preceding operations on January 20th, 2023, Olli 2-18 ran the route as normal with no anomalies. There were no software updates or other system changes before it was run again on January [XXX], 2023, the date of curb contact.
2. The root cause of the curb contact was a communication error with the HD Map registration module. HD Map registration utilizes real-time lidar and positioning data and compares that to a-priori HD maps stored within the autonomy system. A communication problem occurred between the computer running the map registration software and the computer running the navigation algorithms. The cause for the communication problem has been identified and a fix has been implemented to prevent the issue from happening again (see below).
3. Steering was out of calibration. It was noted through data collection that the steering was out of calibration at time of incident. The autonomy system was attempting to correct this issue, but the vehicular steering system could not achieve the required turn radius. This is a vehicular maintenance concern managed by the customer.
It was determined that the HD map registration issue had not been observed during autonomous operations in the previous four years. The solution to prevent further occurrences includes:
1. Implementing a self-diagnostic routine upon system boot, which ensures the communication connection is established. If the connection is not established, this diagnostic will prevent the vehicle from driving autonomously. 
2. Updating the error checks to ensure that during run time, the vehicle will come to a controlled stop in event of a communication problem.  
3. Working with the customer to recalibrate the steering, and assisting in reviewing customer's vehicle maintenance checks for steering calibration if necessary.
4. Continuing to review data to determine other concerns or improvements.

***10-Day Update***
On February 15th, Kia removed the subject 2024MY K5 vehicles ACU and downloaded the EDR data. According to the EDR Report, the driver had SCC set at 85 MPH, which was overridden by the driver applying moderate accelerator pedal directly before impact. The EDR Report recorded steering input by the driver of +30 degrees, then +70 degrees directly before impact, which exceeds the ability of Lane Following Assist. About a half of a second before impact, the stability controls were engaged, which disables SCC. The EDR Report also indicates that the driver was not wearing a seat belt, causing severe loading of the steering wheel, gear shift lever, and other internal components. The driver did not press the brake pedal at any point in the recorded data.
Kia did not identify any vehicle or manufacturing concerns during inspection of the vehicle or review of the EDR data. The cause of the incident appears to be driver error.

The subject vehicle was travelling northbound on [XXX] at a stated speed of 45 MPH with Adaptive Cruise Control(ACC) and Lane Centering (LCF) engaged. The customer stated that she had been driving for 10 hours and that it was raining heavily, with low visibility. The vehicle left the roadway at a rail crossing and came to rest parallel with the railroad tracks with the RH side of the vehicle centered within the tracks. The impact with the tracks deflated all four tires and caused damage to the right front bumper cover. There was also damage reported to certain suspension and steering components and the vehicle undercarriage. There were no airbags deployed and the vehicle was towed from the scene. The customer reported minor injuries and was not provided, nor sought immediate medical attention. During a follow-up conversation, the customer indicated that she came upon a road that turned left and,  because of the heavy rain she did not see the curve.
Subaru inspected the subject vehicle on 3/12/2024. Prior to the inspection, the customer provided a diagram of the scene, indicating that the vehicle had actually been travelling in an east-bound direction and that it was a right-hand turn, not left-hand as originally stated. A site visit indicated that the roadway was a country lane with no lane markings. The curve was a sharp (90-degree) turn to the right signposted with an arrow identifying the direction in which to turn. Though there were no previous signs to indicate the approaching turn, there was a Truck Crossing (W11-10) sign 0.3 miles before the turn to alert motorists in advance of locations where unexpected entries into the roadway, which included a recommended speed of 25 MPH.
[REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION]
Based on the inspection, the data acquired and the customer's narrative, Subaru determined that the customer was likely using the ACC, but not LCF, on a roadway with no markings, during a period of heavy rain and low visibility, at a speed that exceeded the posted and recommended speed limits. The customer failed to notice the approaching sharp turn to the right and did not apply the brakes in time to appropriately slow the vehicle to a speed that would allow it to safely navigate the turn. As a result, the customer lost control of the vehicle, which left the roadway and came to rest on the railroad tracks.

The Pony.ai AV operator proceeded to disengage from autonomous mode to attempt to avoid an accident, however, as the Pony.ai AV vehicle operator attempted to step on the throttle, the Pony.ai AV is rear-ended by Vehicle 2. The Pony.ai AV was stopped at 0 mph, while the approximate speed of Vehicle 2 at the point of collision was 5 mph. The Pony.ai AV operator noted that prior to the collision, the driver of Vehicle 2 appeared to drive erratically across other intersections as well. The contact between the vehicles caused a moderate damage to the back of the Pony.ai AV and moderate damage to Vehicle 2. Both drivers pulled over to the side of the roadway and exchanged information. There were no injuries reported and the police were not called. Pursuant to protocol, Pony.ai ran simulations after the accident to determine if the ADV would have reacted differently. The results indicate the Pony.ai ADV would not have reacted differently.
